source_text: Ἢ οὐκ ἴσμεν ὁπόσοι μὲν ἀγροὶ, πό σαι δὲ οἰκίαι, πόσα δὲ ἔθνη καὶ πόλεις, καὶ ζώντων ἔτι τῶν κτησαμένων, ἑτέρων ὀνόματα μετημφιάσαντο δεσποτῶν; καὶ ὡς οἱ μὲν πάλαι δουλεύοντες ἐπὶ τὸν τῆς ἀρχῆς θρόνον ἀνέβησαν, οἱ δὲ κύριοι καὶ δεσπό ται καλούμενοι στῆναι μετὰ τῶν ἀρχομένων ἠγάπη σαν, καὶ τοῖς ἑαυτῶν δούλοις ὑπέκυψαν, ὥσπερ ἐν κύβων περιτροπαῖς, μεταχθέντων ἄφνω τῶν πραγμάτων αὐτοῖς; Τά γε μὴν εἰς βρῶσιν ἡμῖν ἐπινενοημένα καὶ πόσιν, καὶ πάντα, ὅσα πέρα τῆς χρείας ὁ πλοῦτος ὑβρίζων ἐμηχανήσατο πρὸς θεραπείαν τῆς ἀχαρί στου καὶ μηδὲν στεγούσης γαστρὸς, πότ' ἂν ἡμέτερα γένοιτο, κἂν ἐπαντλῆται διηνεκῶς; Ἅ γε μικράν τινα τῇ γεύσει μόνον ἐναποθέμενα κατὰ τὴν πάροδον ἡδο νὴν, εὐθὺς ὡς ὀχληρὰ καὶ περιττὰ δυσχεραίνομεν, καὶ μετὰ σπουδῆς ἔξω ποι βάλλομεν, ὡς εἰ τοῖς σπλάγχνοις ἐγχρονίσοι, τὰ μέγιστα περὶ τοῦ ζῇν κινδυνεύσοντες. Πολλοῖς γοῦν ὁ κόρος ἤγαγε θάνα τον, καὶ τοῦ μηδενὸς ἀπολαύειν ἔτι γεγένηται πρό ξενος. Κοῖται δὲ ἀσελγεῖς, καὶ βέβηλοι συμπλοκαὶ, καὶ πάντα ὅσα λυττώσης ἔργα καὶ παραφόρου ψυχῆς, οὐχὶ πρόδηλος πάντη ζημία τῇ φύσει, καὶ βλάβη περιφανὴς, καὶ τῶν ἰδίων ὄντως ἑκάστου μᾶλ λον ἀλλοτρίωσίς τε καὶ μείωσις, ἐλαττουμένου τοῦ σώματος ἐν ταῖς μίξεσι, καὶ τῆς γνησιωτάτης καὶ συνεκτικωτάτης τῶν μελῶν ἀποσυλωμένου τροφῆς; Τοιγαροῦν ἑκάστου τῶν ταῖς ἀσελγέσιν ἐγκαλινδηθέντων εὐναῖς, μετὰ τὴν πρᾶξιν εὐθὺς, ὅταν ὁ μὲν τῆς σαρκὸς οἶστρος ἀπομαρανθῇ, πρὸς τὸ βδελυρὸν δὲ ὧν ἐνεχείρησε πέρας ἐλθὼν ὁ νοῦς, ὥσπερ ἐκ μέθης ἢ χειμῶνός τινος, τοῦ λογίσασθαι, ποῖ ποτέ ἐστι, λάβοι σχολὴν, σφοδρός τις εἰσέρχεται τῆς ἀκρασίας μετάμελος. Ἀδρανεστέρου τε γὰρ αἰσθάνεται γεγενη μένου τοῦ σώματος, καὶ πρὸς τὴν τῶν ἀναγκαίων ἐργασίαν νωθροῦ, καὶ παντάπασιν ἀσθενοῦς. Τοῦτο δὴ ἄρα καὶ τοῖς παιδοτρίβαις κατανοήσασιν ὁ τῆς σωφροσύνης ἐν ταῖς παλαίστραις γέγραπται νό μος, ἄσυλα παρὰ τῶν ἡδονῶν τοῖς νεανίσκοις φυλάττων τὰ σώματα, καὶ οὐκ ἐπιτρέπων ἀγωνιζομένοις αὐτοῖς, οὐδὲ ὄσον προσβλέψαι ταῖς λαμπού σαις μορφαῖς, εἴγε ἐθέλοιεν στεφανωθῆναι τὴν κεφα λὴν, ὡς τῆς ἀκρασίας γέλωτα ἀγούσης ἐν τῷ παλαίειν, οὐ στέφανον. Ταῦτα μὲν ὡς ἀλλότρια πάντη καὶ περιττὰ, καὶ οὐδενὸς ἴδια γενέσθαι δυνάμενα, παρατρέχειν καλὸν, τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ἐπιμύσαντας· τῶν δὲ ὄντως ἡμετέρων πρόνοιαν προσήκει ποιεῖσθαι πολλήν. Τί δὲ ὄντως ἡμέτερον; Ψυχή τε, ᾗ ζῶμεν, λεπτή τις οὖσα καὶ νοερὰ, καὶ οὐδὲν δεομένη τῶν βαρυνόντων· καὶ σῶμα, τὸ ταύτῃ δοθὲν ὄχημα πρὸς τὸν βίον παρὰ τοῦ κτί σαντος. Τοῦτο γὰρ ἄνθρωπος· νοῦς ἐνδεδεμένος προσ φόρῳ καὶ πρεπούσῃ σαρκί. Τοῦτο ὑπὸ τοῦ πανσόφου τεχνίτου τῶν ὅλων ἐν τοῖς μητρῴοις ἡμῶν πλάττεται κόλποις. Τοῦτο εἰς φῶς ἐκ τῶν σκοτεινῶν ἐκεί νων θαλάμων ὁ τῶν ὠδίνων ἄγει καιρός. Τοῦτο ἄρ χειν ἐτάχθη τῶν ἐπὶ γῆς. Τούτῳ γυμνάσιον ἀρετῆς ἡ κτίσις ὑφήπλωται. Τούτῳ κεῖται νόμος, μιμεῖσθαι τὸν πλάστην εἰς δύναμιν, καὶ τὴν ἐν οὐρανοῖς εὐταξίαν σκιαγραφεῖν ἐπὶ γῆς. Τοῦτο, ἐντεῦθεν καλούμενον, ἀπανίσταται. Τοῦτο τῷ τοῦ πέμψαντος Θεοῦ παρ ίσταται βήματι.
orientation: Basil continues his argument that wealth and pleasures are alien possessions, now turning to what is genuinely ours: the soul and the body.
pass_a_gloss: Or do we not know how many fields, and how many houses, and how many nations and cities, even while those who acquired them were still living, changed their names to those of other masters? And how those formerly enslaved mounted the throne of rule, while those called lords and masters loved to stand among the ruled, and bowed down to their own slaves, as in turns of dice, when affairs were suddenly transferred for them? As for the things devised for us for eating and drinking, and all that wealth in its insolence contrived beyond need for the service of the thankless stomach that holds nothing back, when would they ever become ours, even if they were poured in continually? These things, depositing only a small pleasure in the taste in passing, we immediately find troublesome and superfluous, and we cast them outside with haste, as if, should they linger in the inward parts, we would be in the greatest danger concerning life. For many, satiety brought death, and became the provider of enjoying nothing any longer. And licentious beds, and profane couplings, and all the works of a raging and frenzied soul, are they not altogether manifest loss to nature, and conspicuous harm, and more than anything else alienation and diminution of what is truly each person's own, the body being diminished in the couplings, and being robbed of the most genuine and most sustaining nourishment of the limbs? Therefore, for each of those who have wallowed in licentious beds, immediately after the act, whenever the sting of the flesh has withered away, and the mind, having come to the end of the loathsome thing it attempted, as if from drunkenness or some storm, should get leisure to consider where in the world it is, a vehement regret for the lack of self-control enters. For he perceives that the body has become weaker, and sluggish toward the work of necessary things, and altogether feeble. This indeed, then, having been observed also by the trainers, the law of self-control has been written in the wrestling schools, keeping the bodies of the young men inviolate from the pleasures, and not permitting them, while competing, even so much as to look upon shining forms, if they wish to be crowned on the head, since lack of self-control brings laughter in wrestling, not a crown. These things, as altogether alien and superfluous, and able to become the property of no one, it is good to run past, having shut the eyes; but of the things truly ours it is fitting to take much forethought. What then is truly ours? The soul, by which we live, being something fine and intellectual, and needing none of the things that weigh down; and the body, the vehicle given to it for life by the creator. For this is a human being: a mind bound in suitable and fitting flesh. This is fashioned by the all-wise craftsman of all things in our motherly wombs. This the time of birth pangs leads into light from those dark chambers. This was appointed to rule over the things on earth. For this the creation has been spread out as a training ground of virtue. For this a law is laid down, to imitate the fashioner as far as possible, and to sketch in outline the good order in the heavens upon earth. This, being called from here, departs. This stands before the judgment seat of the God who sent it.

choices.why: The verb means to change clothing or disguise; here it is used of properties taking on new owners' names, so 'changed their names' captures the transfer of naming.
The verb means to stoop or bow under; Basil uses it to show the reversal of masters becoming subservient to their own slaves.

choices.english: as if, should they linger in the inward parts
choices.why: The conditional εἰ with the optative marks a hypothetical future condition; 'should they linger' preserves the conditional force and the optative mood.
rejected: as if they were to linger

choices.why: The verb means to strip or plunder; 'being robbed' conveys the forceful deprivation of the body's nourishment.
Basil uses this term for the body as the soul's conveyance through life; 'vehicle' is the literal sense and matches the brief's body gloss.
The verb means to paint in shadow or outline; Basil uses it for imitating heavenly order on earth, so 'sketch in outline' keeps the artistic metaphor.

pass_b_english: Or do we not know how many fields, how many houses, how many nations and cities took on the names of other masters while those who acquired them were still alive? And how those who once were slaves climbed onto the throne of rule, while those called lords and masters were content to stand among the governed, and bowed down to their own slaves, as if in a turn of the dice their affairs had suddenly been reversed?

As for the things devised for our eating and drinking, and all that wealth in its insolence has contrived beyond need for the service of the thankless belly that holds nothing back—when could they ever be ours, even if they are poured in continually? They deposit only a small pleasure in the taste as they pass, and immediately we are disgusted with them as troublesome and superfluous, and we eagerly cast them out, as if, should they linger in the inward parts, we would be in the greatest danger for our very life. At any rate, surfeit has brought death to many, and has become the provider of no longer enjoying anything at all.

And licentious beds, and profane embraces, and all the works of a raging and frenzied soul—are they not plainly and entirely a loss to nature, and a conspicuous harm, and rather an alienation and diminishment of what truly belongs to each person, as the body is diminished in its couplings and robbed of the most genuine and sustaining nourishment of its members? Therefore, for each of those who have wallowed in licentious beds, immediately after the act, when the sting of the flesh has withered away and the mind has come to the loathsome end of what it attempted, as if from drunkenness or some storm it finds leisure to consider where on earth it is, a violent regret for its lack of self-control enters in. For it perceives that the body has become weaker, sluggish for the work of necessary tasks, and altogether feeble.

This, then, is what the trainers understood when the law of self-control was written in the wrestling schools, keeping the bodies of the young men inviolate from pleasures, and not permitting them, while they were competing, even to glance at shining faces, if they wished to have their heads crowned—since lack of self-control brings laughter in the wrestling, not a crown.

These things, then, as entirely alien and superfluous, and unable to become the property of anyone, it is good to pass by with eyes shut. But of the things that are truly ours, we ought to take great forethought. What then is truly ours? The soul, by which we live, which is something fine and intellectual, and needs none of the things that weigh it down; and the body, the vehicle given to it for life by the Creator. For this is a human being: a mind bound in suitable and fitting flesh. This is fashioned in our mothers' wombs by the all-wise craftsman of all things. This the time of birth pangs leads into the light from those dark chambers. This was appointed to rule over the things on earth. For this, creation has been spread out as a training ground of virtue. For this, a law is laid down: to imitate the Maker as far as possible, and to sketch in outline on earth the good order of the heavens. This, when it is called from here, departs. This stands before the judgment seat of the God who sent it.

problems.quote: changed their names to other owners
problems.why: Greek says owners changed names (i.e., properties took new owners' names), not that owners changed their own names.
problems.fix: took on the names of other masters
problems.ruling: μετημφιάσαντο ἑτέρων ὀνόματα δεσποτῶν: properties took new owners' names, not owners changed their own names.

problems.quote: more than anything else an alienation and diminishment of what truly belongs to each person
problems.source_quote: καὶ τῶν ἰδίων ὄντως ἑκάστου μᾶλλον ἀλλοτρίωσίς τε καὶ μείωσις
problems.why: μᾶλλον goes with ἀλλοτρίωσις: 'rather an alienation... of one's own things', not 'more than anything else'.
problems.fix: rather an alienation and diminishment of what truly belongs to each person
problems.ruling: μᾶλλον modifies ἀλλοτρίωσίς τε καὶ μείωσις: 'rather an alienation', not 'more than anything else'.

edits.old: changed their names to other owners
edits.new: took on the names of other masters

edits.old: more than anything else an alienation and diminishment of what truly belongs to each person
edits.new: rather an alienation and diminishment of what truly belongs to each person

fixed: Corrected 'changed their names to other owners' to 'took on the names of other masters' to reflect that the properties took on the names of new masters, not that the owners changed their own names.
Corrected 'more than anything else an alienation' to 'rather an alienation' to reflect that μᾶλλον modifies the alienation, not the comparison.

last_rejected.quote: the thankless belly that holds nothing back
last_rejected.source_quote: τῆς ἀχαρίστου καὶ μηδὲν στεγούσης γαστρός
last_rejected.why: μηδὲν στεγούσης means 'holding nothing' i.e. insatiable, not 'holding nothing back'
last_rejected.fix: the thankless belly that holds nothing, insatiable
last_rejected.ruling: στεγούσης can mean 'holding back/concealing'; 'holds nothing back' captures insatiable belly adequately.

last_rejected.quote: the provider of no longer enjoying anything at all
last_rejected.source_quote: τοῦ μηδενὸς ἀπολαύειν ἔτι γεγένηται πρόξενος
last_rejected.why: πρόξενος takes genitive of what is provided; it means 'cause of no longer enjoying anything', not 'provider'
last_rejected.fix: has become the cause of no longer enjoying anything at all
last_rejected.ruling: πρόξενος meaning 'provider/cause of' is within normal range; no meaning is lost.

last_rejected.why: τῇ φύσει is dative of disadvantage: 'a loss for nature' or 'harm to our nature', not abstract 'nature'
last_rejected.ruling: 'A loss to nature' adequately renders ζημία τῇ φύσει; dative of disadvantage need not be explicit.

last_rejected.quote: the most genuine and sustaining nourishment of its members
last_rejected.source_quote: τῆς γνησιωτάτης καὶ συνεκτικωτάτης τῶν μελῶν ἀποσυλωμένου τροφῆς
last_rejected.why: τροφῆς is genitive with ἀποσυλωμένου; 'robbed of the most genuine and cohesive nourishment of its members'
last_rejected.fix: robbed of the most genuine and cohesive nourishment of its members
last_rejected.ruling: 'Sustaining' adequately renders συνεκτικωτάτης ('cohesive'); meaning is preserved without major loss.

last_rejected.quote: as if from drunkenness or some storm it finds leisure to consider where on earth it is
last_rejected.source_quote: ὥσπερ ἐκ μέθης ἢ χειμῶνός τινος, τοῦ λογίσασθαι, ποῖ ποτέ ἐστι, λάβοι σχολήν
last_rejected.why: λάβοι σχολήν is subjunctive/optative of result: 'so that it gets leisure to consider', not 'it finds leisure'
last_rejected.fix: so that, as if from drunkenness or some storm, it gets leisure to consider where on earth it is
last_rejected.ruling: 'Finds leisure' adequately renders λάβοι σχολήν; optative nuance is minor, not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: since lack of self-control brings laughter in the wrestling, not a crown
last_rejected.source_quote: ὡς τῆς ἀκρασίας γέλωτα ἀγούσης ἐν τῷ παλαίειν, οὐ στέφανον
last_rejected.why: ἀγούσης is 'bringing on/producing', but γέλωτα is accusative object; 'since lack of self-control brings on laughter in wrestling, not a crown'
last_rejected.fix: since lack of self-control brings on laughter in the wrestling, not a crown
last_rejected.ruling: 'Brings laughter' adequately renders γέλωτα ἀγούσης; 'brings on' is a minor preference, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: unable to become the property of anyone
last_rejected.why: οὐδενός is genitive: 'unable to become anyone's own', i.e. belong to anyone as their own possession
last_rejected.ruling: 'Property of anyone' correctly renders οὐδενὸς ἴδια; meaning is preserved accurately.

last_rejected.why: λεπτή here means 'subtle, refined, delicate' (of immaterial things), not 'fine' in modern sense; 'subtle and intellectual'
last_rejected.ruling: 'Fine' can mean 'subtle/refined'; within normal range for λεπτή, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: a mind bound in suitable and fitting flesh
last_rejected.source_quote: νοῦς ἐνδεδεμένος προσφόρῳ καὶ πρεπούσῃ σαρκί
last_rejected.why: ἐνδεδεμένος is 'bound in/enclosed in', but 'bound' alone is ambiguous; 'a mind bound up in suitable and fitting flesh'
last_rejected.fix: a mind bound up in suitable and fitting flesh
last_rejected.ruling: 'Bound in' adequately renders ἐνδεδεμένος; 'bound up' is a minor preference, not misleading.
